prime.problem: Every decode step reads every cached key and value. With one K and V head per query head (MHA), Llama-3.1-8B's shape would cache 512 KiB per token and only 14 sequences of 8k would fit on an H100. MQA shares one K/V head for all queries, but loses quality and trains unstably.
prime.fits: First card on making each token's KV smaller. The FlashAttention cards changed how attention is computed; from here the course attacks the bytes per token in the capacity formula, starting with the architectural knob Llama already uses.
expect: G groups: GQA-H = MHA, GQA-1 = MQA
decode intensity ≈ query heads per group
the notation trap: G vs r
prime.goal: Compute KV bytes, sequences that fit and decode throughput for any G, and explain why the paper picks 8 groups over MQA.

attend: What exactly is shared in GQA, and what stays per head?
Why does cutting KV heads 4× give almost exactly 4× decode throughput on a full H100, but 32× gives only 28.9×?
Why does GQA barely raise decode attention's arithmetic intensity toward the 295 ridge?
Why does a converted-but-not-uptrained GQA model do fine, while MQA needs uptraining to be useful?
What does "G" mean in the paper versus perf-2's attention-intensity card, and which is Llama's 4:1?

must: Group H query heads into G groups sharing one K and V head → KV per token = 2·L·G·d_h·b → cache and per-step reads shrink by H/G → Llama's 8 groups: 128 KiB vs MHA's 512 KiB, 59 vs 14 sequences of 8k

A full H100 reads its whole pool every step (~19 ms) → smaller KV means more sequences share each step → throughput tracks the KV cut (4× → 4.0×) → until the batch is so large that matmul FLOPs (7.73 ms at MQA's 476) outweigh the weight read → 32× less KV buys 28.9×

Fewer K/V heads remove capacity the model had → MQA (G = 1) loses quality (−0.6 avg, 53.93 without uptraining) and spikes in training → G = 8 keeps quality within 0.1 of MHA at 5.4× its speed → an intermediate G is the sweet spot
elevated: Each K/V row is reused by r = H/G query heads → decode attention intensity ≈ r (4.00 FLOPs/byte for Llama) → still far below 295 → decode attention stays memory-bound for every G, so bytes, not FLOPs, set the step
reference: Table 1's per-task ROUGE, BLEU and F1 scores
the ms vs s axis quirk
the sharding argument for replicated KV heads

compress.prompt: Draw the three layouts (MHA, GQA-8, MQA) from memory with 8 query heads, then write one causal chain from G to decode throughput and one from G to quality.
checklist: MHA: one K/V per query head; GQA: one per group; MQA: one for all
KV per token ∝ G; cut = H/G
fewer KV bytes → more sequences per full HBM → throughput ∝ cut, until compute-bound
fewer KV heads → less capacity → MQA quality loss; G = 8 ≈ MHA quality

retrieve.q: Explain why GQA shrinks the KV cache without shrinking the number of attention heads the model computes.
answer: query heads stay separate; only K and V projections are shared per group
the cache stores K and V, so it scales with the number of groups
each query head still gets its own attention pattern over the shared K, V

retrieve.q: Walk through the G = 8 row of the card's H100 table: sequences that fit, KV read time, step time, tokens/s.
answer: max(0.96 ms FLOPs, 4.79 ms weights) = 4.79 ms

retrieve.q: You are designing a new model and choosing G. What do you gain and lose going from 8 groups to 1, and when is the gain smaller than the KV cut suggests?
answer: 8× less KV, more sequences, faster decode
quality loss and training instability (loss spikes, divergence)
the gain shrinks once the batch makes the step compute-bound (MQA: 28.9× not 32×), and at short context and small batch weights dominate anyway

compare.q: GQA and MLA both shrink the KV cache at training time. What is fundamentally different about what each one caches, which choice gives MLA both a smaller cache and better quality in DeepSeek's ablation, and what does MLA pay for it?
answer: GQA caches full K and V for fewer heads; MLA caches one 512-dim latent plus a 64-dim RoPE key shared by all heads
per-head K and V are rebuilt from the latent through up-projections that absorption folds into the query and output weights
MLA equals GQA with 2.25 groups in size but beat MHA in DeepSeek's tests
MLA pays more FLOPs per byte in decode, a separate RoPE path and dedicated kernels

compare.q: perf-2 listed GQA as one KV trick. This card adds uptraining and the quality curve. When is "just use fewer KV heads" not available to a serving team, and what do they reach for instead?
answer: G is fixed when the model is trained; Llama-3.1-8B ships with 8
converting needs ~5% of pre-training compute to recover quality
serving teams use FP8 or 2-bit KV and paging instead

predict.q: Move the card's H100 table to 32k context. For G = 2 (hypothetical), how many sequences fit and what is the step time? How does it compare to the real model at 8k? Commit first.
predict.answer: At 32k, G = 2 is 32 KiB × 32,768 = 1.074 GB per sequence, exactly the real G = 8 model's size at 8k. So 59 fit and the step is the same 23.70 ms, 2,489 tokens/s. Context and KV heads trade one for one in the capacity formula (our arithmetic).

apply.task: Extend the card's table to 32k context for G = 32, 8, 2, 1: KV per sequence, sequences that fit in 63.94 GB, step time (B·KV/BW + max(2BP/C, W/BW)) and tokens/s. Then compute MQA's gain over MHA and explain why it's larger than at 8k.
apply.done: You have a four-row table with one line of arithmetic per row, and your MQA/MHA gain matches the card's try-this.
apply.hint: G = 32: 17.18 GB, 3 fit, 20.18 ms, 149 tok/s. G = 8: 4.295 GB, 14, 22.74 ms, 616 tok/s. G = 2: 1.074 GB, 59, 23.70 ms, 2,489. G = 1: 0.537 GB, 119, 23.86 ms, 4,986. MQA/MHA = 33.5×: every row stays weight-bound (the matmuls never exceed 4.79 ms), so the whole cut shows up; it even exceeds 32× because MHA's 3 sequences (51.5 GB) leave part of the pool empty (our arithmetic).
